title: Local magnitude shuffles detect short ordering in Oklahoma M2.5+ events but miss long triggering in three tests
abstract: We test whether larger Oklahoma earthquakes precede nearby smaller events more often than local magnitude shuffles predict. This test does not fit an ETAS decay law. In 10,805 OGS M2.5+ events from 2010 to 2026, the signed pair count at 1-7 days within 10 km is 3.61 exact null standard deviations above its mean. The two-sided randomization p value is 0.001 after correction across five lag bins. Removal of M5+ events leaves a signal (corrected p=0.005). OGS M3+ gives weaker evidence, while ComCat M3+ gives corrected p=0.0026. The catalogs share source data. Later-period subsets give no clear signal. Synthetic 5-day triggering gives a strong short-lag signal, but known 250-day triggering is missed in three examples. We derive the exact conditional null moments and show which components local conditioning removes. The result is consistent with rapid triggering under local magnitude exchangeability. The long-lag null cannot establish a triggering cutoff. This study does not identify the external driver of residual seismicity.

display.caption: Magnitude-order deviations in real catalogs and synthetic checks. Gray shading is plus or minus 1.96 exact null standard deviations, not a simultaneous confidence interval. Lines in panel C are means over three seeds; shading gives their range. Known 250-day triggering has weak order evidence in these examples.
